problemStatement.formal: \exists\, F : [0,1] \to [0,1] \text{ continuous, monotone, surjective, constant on each removed middle-third interval, with } F' = 0 \text{ Lebesgue-a.e., yet } F(1) - F(0) = 1.
problemStatement.plain: The Cantor function, the 'devil's staircase,' is continuous and increasing on [0,1], climbing from 0 to 1, yet it is flat on every open middle-third interval removed in the Cantor construction. Its entire rise is carried on the Cantor set, a set of Lebesgue measure zero, so F' = 0 almost everywhere even though F increases by a full unit. It is the canonical singular continuous function and is currently absent from Mathlib.
whyMatters: It is the standard counterexample separating monotone continuity from absolute continuity: the fundamental theorem of calculus fails since the integral of F' is 0 while F(1) - F(0) = 1.
It is the concrete witness of a nonzero singular measure supported on a Lebesgue-null set, seeding the theory of singular distributions and self-affine functions.
It completes the gallery's Cantor-set story: the parent proof shows the set is an uncountable null set; this builds the function whose entire variation lives on that null set.

open: No construction of the Cantor function F : ℝ → ℝ (or on [0,1]) exists in Mathlib or this gallery.
No formal proof that such an F is continuous, monotone, and surjective onto [0,1], nor constant on each removed middle-third interval.
No formal proof that F' = 0 Lebesgue-almost-everywhere, nor the singularity statement that the integral of F' is 0 while F(1) - F(0) = 1.
knownResults.goal: Construct F and prove its defining properties (continuity, monotonicity, surjectivity onto [0,1], constancy on each removed middle-third interval), then establish F' = 0 Lebesgue-a.e. Stage one: construction plus continuity/monotonicity/surjectivity; stage two: the a.e.-derivative-zero result.
